about: Texts read from outside this house for this work. No source document is committed; build.py fetches each, asserts the PDF's hash, and finds each passage (in the 1977 scan by its letters, since the scan is two columns read through OCR; in the abstracts and the Unicode annex word for word).

sources.cite: Richard E. Nisbett and Timothy DeCamp Wilson, 'Telling More Than We Can Know: Verbal Reports on Mental Processes', Psychological Review 84 (3), 1977, 231–259. doi:10.1037/0033-295X.84.3.231
sources.read: 2026-11-19, in full, as this cycle's reach outside (experimental social psychology, a field this practice had not used). The university's own repository (hdl:2027.42/92167) served a page instead of the file; this copy is a scan of the journal pages.

passages.text: if the reports of subjects do not differ from the reports of observers, then it is unnecessary to assume that the former are drawing on "a fount of privileged knowledge"
passages.where: section on a priori causal theories, quoting Bem (1967, p. 186)

passages.text: It seems equally clear that subjects and observers are drawing on a similar source for their verbal reports about stimulus effects.
The only mystery is why people are so poor at telling the difference between private facts that can be known with near certainty and mental processes to which there may be no access at all.
passages.where: section 'Why are we unaware of our unawareness?'

sources.cite: Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni, Elizabeth Barnes, Yoshua Bengio and 37 others, 'Chain of Thought Monitorability: A New and Fragile Opportunity for AI Safety', arXiv:2507.11473 (2025)
